# Framework Learnings

The methodology's own framework learnings, recorded as the canonical repo dogfoods itself. This
file is the companion to [`SESSION_RUNNER.md`](SESSION_RUNNER.md) — Phase 3C routes every session
to the right learnings home, and for a framework-level learning that home is here.

**Canonical methodology repo:** append a new row at Phase 3C — **append only; do not edit existing
rows.** The rows below are real framework learnings, not placeholders.

**Budget the row before writing it — 1,500 B, checked by `bin/check-learnings`.** A partial read of
this table returns whole rows, because a row is one physical line, so row size is what a session
actually spends here: measured over 80 transcripts of the canonical repo, this file was read whole
once and read in part 243 times. The check covers only rows not yet frozen in git HEAD — the one row
you may still edit. Say it shorter rather than raising the budget.

> **`#14` is reserved, and the gap between 13 and 15 is deliberate — do not close it by renumbering.**
> It is held by `docs/operator-gated-review-plan`'s D3, a branch from the *upstream* session sequence
> that is not present in every clone. S34 verified the reservation is attributable and respected it;
> S35 appended at **15** for the same reason. Renumbering would break every existing `Learning #N`
> citation, which is exactly what "append only, never renumber" exists to prevent.

**Adopter projects:** do **not** edit this file. Like `SESSION_RUNNER.md` it is synced from
canonical and must stay byte-identical, or local edits will block future syncs (see
[`BOOTSTRAP.md`](BOOTSTRAP.md), "Customizations Go in CLAUDE.md, Not in Synced Files"). Record
project learnings in your `CLAUDE.md` → **Project-Specific Methodology Adaptations** →
**Project-specific Learnings** subsection instead.

| # | Learning | Source | When to Apply |
|---|----------|--------|---------------|
| 1 | Plan-mode output is a draft, not a verified plan. When a prompt contains a multi-phase plan with "implement," the deliverable is a plan document with evidence-based inventory, not Phase 1 code. The gap: Phase 1's task mapping had no entry for plan-mode handoffs, so the session defaulted to "implement." Structural fix: new mapping row + FM #19. | FM #19 discovery | When a prompt contains a multi-phase plan with "implement" — recognize this as a planning workstream. |
| 2 | **Protocol discipline is perishable.** 14 consecutive clean sessions can collapse to 1/10 deliveries within 12 hours of relaxed discipline. The protocol is perishable — it doesn't maintain itself. Each session must actively re-internalize it, not assume it's "already known." The compounding loop works only when every link in the chain is complete. | Field observation | Whenever you catch yourself thinking "I know the protocol, I don't need to re-read it" — re-read it. The fast-collapse case (FM #17 slow-drip's sibling) is real. |
| 3 | Plans should flag "here be dragons" areas where implementation is non-obvious — not all phases are equally risky. Call out which phases need extra caution, what assumptions are load-bearing, and where the executor should stop and re-orient. | Field observation | When writing any multi-phase plan. A plan that presents all phases as equally tractable lies to the executor about where the cost actually lives. |
| 4 | **Verify a plan's output against its completion criteria — not against session duration or count.** Execution speed is not evidence of plan quality, and "fits in one session" is not a planning goal. A plan whose phases each fit cleanly in one session and produce work that matches the completion criteria is high-quality; a plan that tempts the executor to bundle phases or skip close-out to "finish faster" is not. The "1 and done" rule does not bend for high-quality plans. | Field observation (refined from rmsharp feedback on issue #7) | When evaluating a plan or judging plan quality. Resist the temptation to read execution speed as plan quality — they are uncorrelated when the protocol holds. |
| 5 | Code review is a distinct deliverable, not overhead. Reviews that produce actionable plans (exact code snippets, line numbers, implementation order) have higher ROI than vague "this needs improvement" feedback. A review that doesn't identify specific changes a future session can execute is incomplete. | Field observation | When the session deliverable is a code review. Output an actionable plan, not a critique. |
| 6 | A plan written from memory of a file read is an assumption-level claim. Reading implementations before estimating complexity catches wrong assumptions early — estimating from a backlog description alone is unreliable. This is a special case of FM #11 (gaps from memory) and FM #20 (edit from memory) applied to planning. | Field observation | Before estimating effort or scope for any phase, read the actual implementation file. The backlog description is a hint, not a spec. |
| 7 | **Cross-reference completeness at self-review.** When a change adds a citation, an index entry, a glossary term, or any cross-reference between files — and especially when it modifies a numbered set (FMs, principles, phases, anti-patterns, learnings) — `git diff` confirms only the present-side edit; the defect is the *absence* on the destination side, which the diff cannot surface. Grep each cited destination to confirm the citation resolves, and grep nearby prose for set-size or named-membership assertions ("N failure modes", "the three workstreams") that may have drifted. Bidirectional: a new index entry needs its destination to cite back; a grown numbered set needs its size claims re-counted. | Three v2.6 instances: stale "24 failure modes" count, understated `/diagnose` + `/grill-with-docs` citation rows, aspirational `/init` citation (issue #19) | When a change touches any cross-file citation, index, glossary term, or numbered set. At self-review, grep destinations and size claims before committing — do not rely on `git diff` alone. |
| 8 | **A close-out gate is only as strong as the weakest checklist that summarizes close-out.** Session-type procedures (Planning, Review/Audit, Debugging, the vertical-slice revert, and campaign per-session checklists) each restate the close-out in condensed form. An agent following a condensed checklist never re-reads the full phase, so any cross-cutting gate the summary omits is silently exempted for that session type — exactly how an "authoritative" ledger acquires holes. When you add or change a close-out step, reconcile it into *every* checklist that restates close-out, not only the canonical Phase 3/Phase 6 text. This is Learning #7 applied to procedure summaries rather than citations. | FM #27 / escape #8 (CHANGELOG-ledger campaign, S7) | When adding or modifying any close-out or other cross-cutting gate: grep every session-type and campaign checklist that restates close-out and confirm the new step appears in each. |
| 9 | **A handoff is only dependable when it is a durable, machine-checkable artifact.** A transient narrative — spoken, or written only to the wholesale-overwritten `SESSION_NOTES.md` — leaves no evidence of its own absence, so a skipped close-out report is invisible until a human notices (the failure that motivated the receipt: an agent had to be *prompted* for its report). The fix mirrors the ledger (FM #27) exactly: **gate-on-write** (a `HANDOFFS.md` receipt whose structure `bin/check-handoff` verifies) **AND reconcile-on-read** (Phase 0 greps for a missing/`status: pending` receipt and backfills it `status: reconciled`) — neither is dependable alone. The honest ceiling is the same too: the check verifies presence and structure, never quality (a green check is not a good handoff), and a session that leaves no commit and no 1B stub still escapes. This is Learning #8 applied to the report itself, not just the ledger. | Close-out receipt slice (this session) | When adding any close-out artifact or gate: make it a durable, greppable artifact with a write-gate AND a reconcile-on-read backstop — never a transient note or a spoken summary. |
| 10 | **A review pass scoped to the diff has a blind spot: what the change made stale *outside* it.** Learning #7 (cross-reference completeness) and Learning #8 (close-out-gate propagation) are authoring-time self-checks — they catch drift the *author* introduces. But an adversarial review or audit is pointed at the diff by default, so "what did this change make stale elsewhere in the corpus?" is nobody's job. The v3.3 close-out-receipt work (#52/#53) shipped a clean 6-lens adversarial review, yet left `HOW_TO_USE.md`, the `README.md` repo tree, and three tutorials describing close-out *without* the new receipt — none were in the diff, so no diff-scoped lens looked at them. A human had to ask "has documentation been fully updated?" (fixed in #54). | Upstream issue #55 (completeness-critic proposal), motivated by the v3.3 doc-completeness gap fixed in PR #54 | Promote Learning #7/#8 from an authoring self-check to a review-time lens: when a change adds, renames, or removes a concept, artifact, file, step, or numbered-set member, grep the *whole corpus* (not just the diff) for file/artifact enumerations, worked examples/tutorials, indexes/cross-references, and count/size claims ("N failure modes", "the six requirements") that now lag. See `workstreams/AUDIT_WORKSTREAM.md`'s Verification Checklist for the operative step. |
| 11 | **Heterogeneous capability tiers within one slice are a division of labor, not a new gate.** Splitting a pre-declared vertical slice's layers across agents of different capability tiers — with the strongest tier reviewing every lighter-tier layer's output before that layer's checkpoint commit lands — satisfies the existing per-boundary verification gates (c)/(d); it does not add a fifth gate or substitute for the build/test matrix. The risk is a plausible-sounding misreading: treating cross-tier review as proof a layer is correct on its own, or batching review to the end of the slice instead of per boundary — either one reopens failure mode #26 (mega-session masquerading as a vertical slice) wearing a division-of-labor costume. | The close-out-receipt slice's own hybrid capability-tier build (`HANDOFFS.md` session S1; concrete agent/model names live in `RECOMMENDED_SKILLS.md`), formalized as the §Vertical Slice Sessions "capability-tiered review" addition (BL-7) | When a slice's layers will be built or reviewed by agents of different capability tiers: state the tier assignment in the gate (a) contract, delegate a layer only where an objective gate (test suite, exhaustive grep, mechanical spec) proves its correctness, and confirm review happens per boundary before each checkpoint commit — never as one pass at the end. |
| 12 | **When an invariant is mechanical, encode it as a test — a review-time grep is a human step that silently stops happening.** Learnings #7 and #10 catch stale cross-references by *grepping at review time*, and that is the right tool for a relation between prose and meaning. But where the invariant is a relation between two **enumerable sets**, the grep is a weak substitute for an assertion: it depends on someone remembering, and its absence leaves no evidence. The motivating case: `HANDOFFS.md` joined the distributed corpus in v3.3 and was never added to the health scanner's methodology checklist, so the checklist silently stopped describing the corpus it scores — and the gap survived *two* releases of exactly the greps #7 and #10 prescribe. Stated as a property of two lists ("every distributed adopter-root destination is either on the checklist or explicitly exempt with a stated reason"), it is a few lines of test code — plus a second test that guards the guard, asserting every exemption names a real distributed file and states a reason, so a stale exemption cannot quietly hollow the invariant out. Once written, the whole class is closed: the next distributed artifact fails the suite instead of going uncounted. **The precondition is non-negotiable — drive the new assertion RED against unpatched code and watch it fail before trusting it.** A mechanized invariant that was never seen to fail is the same trap one level up, and this campaign hit it twice: an absence-check filtering a *dict* by `"Large files" in r` tested keys and passed vacuously, and a fixture whose render toolchain short-circuited the counts under test was structurally incapable of failing while looking like coverage. Pair every absence assertion with a presence control, and ask what a fixture makes *unreachable*, not only what it asserts. | Dashboard signal-integrity campaign (S9–S16) — the manifest-vs-checklist guard prototyped in S9 and shipped in Layer 1; the two vacuous tests caught in Layer 7 | When a change adds a member to an enumerable distributed set (a shipped file, a checklist item, a numbered set), or when you are about to rely on #7/#10 to keep two lists in step: ask whether the invariant is a relation between two sets you can enumerate in code. If it is, write the assertion — then drive it RED before trusting it. Keep the grep for what cannot be enumerated. |
| 13 | **A forward-looking claim cannot be checked by re-reading a file — it has to be computed.** Learning #6 and FM #11 catch claims written *from memory*, and both prescribe the same repair: re-read the file that confirms it. #7, #10 and #12 catch cross-references that go stale *in the corpus*. Neither reaches a handoff's predictions. "Expect one merge conflict", "these are the files you will touch", "this should be quick" describe a state that does not exist yet, so no file confirms them; the only honest check is to derive the answer, or to say plainly that it is a guess. The case in the Source column did not go stale — that is the tempting diagnosis and the wrong one; it was never true. A wrong prediction is worse than none: it licenses the successor to resolve *quickly* rather than *carefully*, and a merge resolved on the belief that "only the ledger differs" discards work silently, with no failing check to catch it. | This repo's v3.6 release cycle — a receipt predicted one conflicting file and the merge met seven; the sentence was written in a commit that had itself changed all seven | When you *write* a claim about a state that does not exist yet — a merge outcome, the files the next session will touch, an effort estimate — derive it or label it a guess. For a merge the derivation is exact and touches no working tree: `git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only <ours> <theirs>` lists the conflicting paths between the tree id on line 1 and the trailing `CONFLICT` block. When you *inherit* a prediction, re-derive it before acting. |
| 15 | **A "nothing was lost" proof must quantify over the PARTITION, not the total — a whole-set check is structurally blind to misplacement.** When content is split across two artifacts (a ledger and its archive, a file and its extraction, a table and its sibling), the natural proof is *reassemble the pieces and compare to the original*. It is necessary and it is not sufficient: **moving content from one half to the other is exactly preserving under reassembly**, so the check cannot see it. This is not hypothetical — it happened here. A split published a byte-for-byte whole-file `md5` reconstruction, correctly, in the same commit that relocated a file-scoped paragraph out of the file that declared it; the proof passed because the paragraph was still *somewhere*, and the paragraph is still missing. The failure is worse in newest-on-top files, where file-scoped trailing content sits at the bottom — precisely the region an oldest-first cut takes from — so it migrates *by position* unless something pins it. **The repair:** classify the artifact into zones before splitting (what is partitionable vs. what is file-scoped), then assert each zone separately — *every byte of the pinned zones is still in THIS file and absent from the other* — alongside the reassembly check, never instead of it. Scope the reassembly check to the partitionable zone only, or it will contradict any legitimate regeneration and refuse every run. **Also: publish the payload BOUNDARY and the COMMAND beside any digest.** A hash whose payload definition is unrecorded cannot be re-derived by a successor — one here resisted five reconstruction attempts — which makes it an assertion wearing a proof's clothes. | S35 (2026-08-03), designing the ledger trimmer: derived from three hand-performed archive events, one of which lost content while its proof passed | Any split, extraction, archive, migration, or de-duplication that moves records between artifacts. The tell is a verification that compares totals — counts, sizes, digests, "N in, N out" — rather than asserting where each part landed. |
| 16 | **Wire the assertion to the ARTIFACT, not to the inputs you built it from — and beware a mutation score earned by mutating the predicate.** Learning #12 says: encode a mechanical invariant as a test, and drive it RED before trusting it. Both halves can be satisfied while the guard is inert, because #12 is about whether the assertion *is correct* and says nothing about *what it is handed*. A checker fed `parts` and `whole` that were derived from each other asserts an identity: `records[:k] ++ records[k:] == records` is true for every input, so the guard cannot fail no matter how badly the code between the split and the write corrupts things. The tell is that the operands are computed, not read back. **The repair is one line of discipline: re-parse what you are about to write, with the same grammar you will read it with, and assert over THAT.** The second half is sharper and more general: a mutation harness inherits the same blind spot. Mutating each predicate and watching the suite go red proves the predicates are correct *as functions*; it proves nothing about whether they are connected to anything. Mutate the **producer** — the code that builds the artifact — not only the **checker**. A harness that mutates only checkers can report a perfect score over guards that are all tautologies. | S36 (2026-08-03), building the ledger trimmer: a 13-mutant harness killed 13/13 while all three losslessness assertions were identities at their only call site; a write path that silently dropped a record was written with `[L1_OK] [L2_OK] [L3_OK]`, and only the independently generated proof script caught it | Whenever a checker and the thing it checks are produced by the same run — losslessness proofs, round-trip/idempotence checks, reconciliation, migration verifiers, invariant assertions over a transform. Ask two questions: *where did each operand come from?* (if both were computed from the same source, the check is an identity) and *does my mutation set include the producer, or only the checker?* |
| 17 | **When a spec demands both "read the value from X" and "assert your value equals X's", those are not two requirements — they are a contradiction, and the falsifiability of the owed test settles which half to build.** A ratified design said the consumer should *read* a number from the tool that owns it, and in the same paragraph made the session owe an agreement test that the displayed number *equals* that tool's. Read the first clause literally and the second is an identity over one value: it passes forever, cannot fail, and certifies nothing — Learning #16 one level up, with the tautology written into the **specification** rather than into a test. The resolution is not to read the sentence harder or to pick the clause you prefer: **implement whichever reading leaves the owed test able to go red**, which here meant computing independently and reading only the one input that is genuinely the other tool's to own (a calibrated constant, parsed from its source by regex). Then verify the test discriminates by making the two sides disagree on purpose — three separate divergences did, and every one of them was a real defect the agreement would otherwise have hidden. **Corollary, and the reason this is not merely elegant:** an agreement that holds only because of the current repo's history is not an agreement. Every archive shard here happened to shrink its ledger, so a missing filter agreed by luck; the divergence appeared only on a fixture built to break it. Ask what accident of *this* corpus is holding the two sides together, and build the case that removes it. | S38 (2026-08-03), the trim-trigger dashboard row: design §1.3 asked for both, and the agreement test was the tiebreaker | Any time a design says one component should consume another's value AND that the two must be shown to agree — dashboards over tools, caches over sources, denormalised fields over their origin, a re-implementation kept "in sync" with a reference. |
| 18 | **Prose that instructs a user is an assertion about behaviour — verify it by RUNNING the artifact, never by reading the spec that authorised it.** Learning #16 says wire a *test* to the artifact rather than to the inputs it was built from; this is its documentation sibling, and it bites harder because prose has no red state to fail into. A ratified design said the tool would leave its work *"staged-but-uncommitted"*. The shipped tool contains no `git add` anywhere, prints `WRITTEN (uncommitted — this tool never commits)`, and leaves the file it creates **untracked**. That sentence was copied faithfully out of the spec and into a **distributed** template, where it would have told every adopter their change was staged — so an ordinary `git commit -a` would have landed the *shortened* ledger while the archive holding the removed records never entered history at all. That is exactly the loss the tool's three losslessness assertions exist to prevent, invited by the documentation rather than by the code. The spec was not lying; it was **stale**, and its own rollback table two lines below already contradicted it. **The test: for every behavioural sentence you ship, name the command whose output you watched. If the honest answer is "the design says so", you have cited an intention, not a behaviour.** The same session shipped a second instance in the same file — a worked anecdote about the repo's own history whose causal order was **inverted**, inferred from two same-day timestamps and settled in one command (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`). A narrative is a claim: it needs its command exactly as a number does. | S40 (2026-08-04), the ledger-doctrine seed sections: `--write`'s seed text claimed the trimmer "leaves the change staged for you" (copied verbatim from `ledger-trimmer-design.md:722`), but the shipped tool has no `git add` anywhere, prints `WRITTEN (uncommitted — this tool never commits)`, and leaves the new shard untracked | Before shipping any behavioural sentence in a spec, seed, or distributed template — what a tool leaves staged, tracked, committed, or otherwise does — run the artifact and watch what it actually does; do not carry the spec's claim forward unverified. Applies equally to narrative claims about causal order (*this happened before that*) — settle them with a command, not inferred timestamps. |
| 19 | **A version tripwire keyed to something that never changes across versions cannot fire — and it fails by reporting *current*, which is worse than reporting nothing.** A stale-format detector compared each adopter-owned template against a marker string, and the markers were the files' H1 titles. Titles are wonderfully stable, which is why they were chosen — and stability is exactly half of what a version marker needs. The other half is that it must be **absent from the versions it has to detect**, and a title that has never changed is absent from nothing. So when the template format did change, every project on the old format was inspected, matched, and reported **current**. The check ran. It returned a confident, wrong answer, and a written promise elsewhere in the corpus ("the format lag is surfaced rather than silent") quietly became false with no test failing. It is the same defect as a guard no mutation can kill, one level down — in *data* rather than code: there, a line no mutant can falsify is a comment shaped like a guard; here, a key no version change can falsify is a constant shaped like a version check. **The test: name a past version the marker would have caught. If you cannot, the marker is decorative.** And accept the consequence rather than designing around it — a discriminating marker must MOVE whenever the format materially changes, so pin it with a case that goes red when it hasn't. A marker that never needs maintenance is a marker that never fires. | S41 (2026-08-04), the URL-update-path fix: `SEED_FORMAT_MARKERS` keyed each distributed seed's stale-format check on its own H1 title — lifetime-stable and therefore non-discriminating — so every adopter already on the old format matched as "current"; measured against 11 sibling projects holding `CHANGELOG.md` and 9 holding `HANDOFFS.md`, none of which carried the new doctrine, all reporting `present` | When designing or reviewing any version/format/staleness tripwire: name a past version the marker would actually have caught. If you cannot, the marker is decorative — key it on something provably absent from the versions it must detect, and pin it with a case that goes red when the format changes but the marker hasn't moved. |
| 20 | **Reviewing independently-generated candidates does not review their SYNTHESIS — grafting pieces from multiple reviewed designs creates a new, unreviewed artifact.** A multi-candidate panel (fresh agents, no shared state, scored by independent judges on independent lenses) is a legitimate way to surface tradeoffs, and its judges genuinely did verify their assigned candidate against the real source rather than trusting its prose. But when the chosen design **synthesizes** — grafts one candidate's mechanism onto a different candidate's sub-component, rather than simply picking one candidate whole — the graft is a combination none of the judges ever saw: their coverage was over each candidate *in isolation*, never over the seam where two candidates' pieces meet. That seam is exactly where a defect can live that neither source candidate's own review would ever surface, because in each candidate alone the pieces that collide here didn't exist together. **The tell: ask what the judges actually scored.** If the answer is "each candidate as its own author wrote it" and the shipped design is not identical to any single candidate, the judging pass has zero coverage of the thing that will actually ship. **The repair is a second, independent review pass scoped to the ACTUAL SYNTHESIZED ARTIFACT** — not a re-score of the candidates, a fresh look at the combination itself, ideally by a differently-shaped process (a hand-trace, a citation re-verification, a completeness re-derivation) than the one that produced it, so it isn't just re-running the same lens that already missed the seam. | S57 (2026-08-09), the issue #67 fork-side fix plan: a 3-candidate/6-judge design panel scored every candidate in isolation and synthesized a design grafting one candidate's target-scoping mechanism with a different candidate's `.gitignore`-aware gate; a second, independent adversarial-review pass against the finished synthesis (not the candidates) found a HIGH-severity defect living exactly in that graft — the gate silently degraded to unconditional whenever the new target-scoping mechanism pointed at a directory that wasn't yet a git repository — invisible to any review of either source candidate alone | Whenever a design, plan, or fix synthesizes (grafts, does not merely select) pieces from multiple independently-reviewed candidates, proposals, or PRs: budget a separate review pass against the actual combined artifact before treating panel/judge scores as coverage — they cover the ingredients, never the recipe. |
| 21 | **A "make it shorter" instruction can be satisfied by moving a metric CORRELATED with size while leaving the actual target metric flat — and a verifier built to catch dropped facts has no way to flag a candidate that dropped nothing and shortened nothing real.** A compaction workflow was asked to shrink `HANDOFFS.md` receipt prose; its instructions targeted a LINE-COUNT reduction ("~40-60% of the original line count"), because the triggering symptom was a line-count cap. Every candidate satisfied it — by removing the original's hand-wrapped line breaks and returning the same prose as one long paragraph. Character count fell 0.0–0.6% on most receipts (one fell from 2,458 to 2,457 characters) while line count fell from 27 to 3. The adversarial verifier, correctly built to catch facts present in the original but missing from the candidate, had no way to object: "lossless" and "reformatted-not-compacted" are not opposites, so a checker built for the first says nothing about the second, and 150 agents' worth of work passed every check while achieving almost nothing. The defect surfaced only because the actual downstream constraint was a BYTE budget, not the line cap the first pass's target happened to share vocabulary with, and a direct character-count measurement — not trust in "fewer lines" — exposed the gap before anything was committed. **The tell: when an instruction says "shorter," ask which unit the downstream problem is actually measured in, and verify THAT unit moved, not a plausible proxy for it.** The repair generalizes: instruct and measure in the target's own unit, and add an explicit "reformatting alone doesn't count" constraint whenever a transformation could satisfy the letter of an instruction (fewer lines) without touching what a downstream consumer actually reads (total bytes, total distinct facts, total tokens). | S61 (2026-08-09), the `HANDOFFS.md` lossless trim: a 39-receipt compact+verify Workflow pass instructed by a line-count target achieved ~1.4% real (character) reduction while reporting apparent success (fewer lines, zero adversarial-verify failures on the reduction dimension); redone with an explicit character-count target and a "line-unwrapping isn't compaction" constraint, real reduction rose to 4.7% | Any time an agent or workflow is asked to make an artifact smaller/shorter/more compact and success is checked only for correctness/losslessness, never for the target metric's actual movement — compaction passes, summarization, log-trimming, "tighten this prose" edits, migrations claiming reduced boilerplate. |
| 22 | **A completed item's own TEXT can be load-bearing for a sibling item's meaning — removing it silently orphans a reference, with no test to catch it.** Phase 3F's "remove a completed backlog item in the same commit" assumes each item is independently deletable. Two adopters' `BACKLOG.md` files falsified that, independently, with different completion markers (wsfct's `🟢 CLEARED` prefix, nprcgenekeepr's `- [x]` checkbox): both had grown cross-references between items — by relative position ("the item above", "immediately below") or by an item's own quoted title — where a completed item was the target a still-OPEN item's reference resolved against. A naive marker-grep-and-delete pass would have corrupted live work in both: wsfct kept 2 of 15 flagged rows, nprcgenekeepr 5 of 9, found only by grepping the *whole file* for positional/quoted references before deleting, not by checking each candidate's own neighbors. nprcgenekeepr's case chained three items (A→B→C, each "immediately below" the last) — removing any proper subset breaks it — plus one chain member was also quoted by name from outside the chain. **The tell:** before deleting, grep the whole file for relative-position language and the item's own quoted phrase. **The repair:** a mutually-referencing cluster is safe to remove only as a whole; an item quoted from outside the cluster blocks removing it alone. | Cross-repo adopter maintenance, 2026-08-10 — wsfct `BACKLOG.md` cleanup (13/15 rows removed) and nprcgenekeepr `BACKLOG.md` cleanup (4/9 items removed), both ad hoc, not numbered sessions in either adopter's sequence | Before removing any completion-flagged item from `BACKLOG.md` (Phase 3F) or a similarly list-shaped ledger with independently-authored entries — grep the whole file for relative-position phrasing and the item's own quoted title, not just its local neighbors. |
| 23 | **A backlog/issue item naming a defect is a claim frozen at filing time, not a live read of current system behavior — unrelated work between filing and actioning can obsolete it without anyone updating the record.** `church_growth/BACKLOG.md` flagged `detect_doc_only()`'s self-referential source-LOC miscount (found 2026-07-21) as needing a future canonical-repo fix. Unrelated work — a different campaign, four commits — had already shipped the exact fix four days later (Layer 7, `ae9e5b7` et al., 2026-07-25). The backlog item's own text was never revised and carried forward unchanged for two weeks, through a cross-repo audit (S70) that named it as "ready-to-act" without re-deriving whether the defect still reproduced. An empirical re-test against the CURRENT canonical scanner — not a re-read of the backlog prose, not trust in the item's own "not fixable from this repo" tag — found the defect gone: `source loc` 0 after vendor reclassification, `detect_doc_only()` returning `is_doc_only=True` even with the local override marker removed. The deliverable inverted from "implement the fix" to "correct the stale record." **The tell:** an item's age relative to the current `HEAD` is itself a signal — the longer a defect-report has sat unactioned, the more likely something else already touched the code path it names. **The repair:** before implementing a fix a backlog item, issue, or carried-forward `next_steps` requests, re-derive whether the named defect still reproduces against CURRENT code (run the check, don't read the claim) — a backlog item is a snapshot, not a live oracle. | S71 (2026-08-10), verifying `church_growth/BACKLOG.md:4-20`: the requested canonical-repo fix had already shipped 2026-07-25, unbeknownst to the two-week-old backlog text that kept requesting it | Before spending a session implementing a fix that a backlog item, issue, or handoff `next_steps` claims is still needed — re-verify the defect reproduces against the current codebase first; do not treat the item's text as ground truth of present behavior just because no one has marked it resolved. |
